description: Skills we are looking for: 3D graphics or animation, UI/UX design, testing and quality assurance, and anyone with a passion for space science or education. Beginners who are eager to learn are welcome.
summary:
We developed Mission Control: Beyond Earth, a browser-based strategy and simulation game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Space Mission Design Game.” Players act as mission directors. They choose one of four missions (the Moon, Mars, the asteroid Bennu, or Earth orbit), design a spacecraft across seven component categories that include real NASA LRO instruments, and balance mass, power, budget, trajectory and risk before launch. During flight, they respond to events such as solar storms and signal loss, and each mission ends with a score and a rank.

The game answers the challenge by turning real engineering trade-offs into decisions that players make and live with. It is grounded in NASA data: live feeds from DONKI, NeoWs and NASA POWER shape space-weather risk, asteroid activity and launch-day weather, while archived NASA sources, including planetary fact sheets, PDS instrument records and Deep Space Network standards, set the physical rules. Players can play alone or in squads of two to four, where each member holds a crew role.

This matters because many students, especially in lower middle-income countries, have computer labs but no access to space engineering. Our game brings a mission design experience to any browser.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Control: Beyond Earth is a browser-based space mission strategy and simulation game. The player becomes a mission director at a NASA-style flight control center and takes a mission from idea to launch and through flight. Every mission follows the same stages as a real one:

  1. Briefing: Choose one of four missions: Lunar Explorer, Mars Pathfinder, Asteroid Surveyor to Bennu, or Earth Observer. Each briefing shows real target data such as gravity, distance and radiation.
  2. Spacecraft design: Build the spacecraft from seven component categories, including real NASA LRO instruments with their actual mass and power figures. The game warns the player immediately when the design is too heavy, short of power or over budget.
  3. Launcher and trajectory: Select a launch vehicle and flight path. Each choice changes cost, travel time and risk.
  4. Launch: Launch-day weather and space weather decide whether the launch is GO, MARGINAL or NO-GO. Bad conditions can scrub the launch or cause a failure.
  5. Mission operations: During flight, players respond to events such as solar storms, signal loss and equipment faults.
  6. Debrief: Each mission is scored from 0 to 100 and earns a rank of Survivor, Specialist or Legend, with a clear explanation of what went well and what failed.

Individual play: A single player can complete every mission alone, making all decisions at their own pace. This suits self-learners and classroom exercises.

Teamwork: Players can form a squad of two to four. Each member takes one or more of twenty crew roles, such as Flight Director or Propulsion Engineer, and only the holder of a role can make that role’s decisions. The game suggests the best role combination for the team, and a live squad chat supports coordination. All squad decisions are checked and saved on the server, so the team shares one consistent mission. This reflects how real missions depend on specialists working together.

NASA data

  • Live, through NASA APIs: DONKI provides recent solar flares, coronal mass ejections and geomagnetic storms that raise mission risk. NeoWs provides today’s near-Earth asteroids for the asteroid mission. NASA POWER, cross-checked with Open-Meteo, gives real launch-pad weather.
  • Collected from NASA archives: NSSDC Planetary Fact Sheets for the Moon, Mars and Earth; six LRO instruments from the Planetary Data System; profiles of real missions such as LRO, Apollo 11, Mars 2020 and OSIRIS-REx; Deep Space Network standards for communication logic; and Blue Marble and SRTM imagery for the 3D Earth.
  • Every source is listed in a Data Sources screen and a Data Explorer, and non-NASA data is clearly marked.

Benefits

  • Players learn gravity, radiation, power, communication and budgeting by making decisions, not by memorizing facts.
  • No special hardware or installation is needed. The game runs in any modern browser on a computer, tablet or phone.
  • Teachers can use it as a ready-made classroom activity, and science clubs can play it together as teams.
  • Real data makes each session different and connects learning to what is happening in space today.

Intended impact

Our research suggests that in many lower middle-income countries, schools and universities have computer labs but no space engineering facilities. Our goal is to give these students, teachers and young researchers a space mission lab in a browser, build interest in space careers from an early age, and help today’s players become tomorrow’s engineers.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: TypeScript, SQL, HTML and CSS
  • Frontend: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, Framer Motion, Three.js for 3D Earth, hangar and launch scenes, and Zustand for game state
  • Backend: Supabase (PostgreSQL, row-level security, server-side functions and Realtime for squad play and chat), with Zod for data validation
  • Data: NASA DONKI, NeoWs and POWER APIs, NASA archive data, Open-Meteo and CelesTrak
  • Hosting: Vercel
  • Hardware: None required beyond a standard device with a web browser

Creativity

  • Real engineering constraints are turned into game mechanics: mass, power and budget become puzzles, and weather and space weather become live risks.
  • Live NASA data means that a real solar storm today can change the outcome of a mission in the game today.
  • Role-based squad play mirrors a real mission control room, where no single person controls everything.
  • Dramatic moments such as weather scrubs, launch failures and explosions make the consequences of each decision memorable.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: a browser-only game that works on low-cost devices
  • Scientific accuracy: values taken from NASA sources, with every source cited inside the game
  • Ease of learning: clear warnings, simple language and explanations in the debrief, so no aerospace background is needed
  • Fairness and reliability: team decisions are verified on the server, so results cannot be altered
  • Engagement: short missions, scores and ranks that encourage players to try again and improve
  • Classroom use: activities that suit both individual learning and group work
